plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000055) on Stephanie Kwolek and Kevlar: the 1965 cloudy polymer solution, persuading a technician to spin it, the strong light fibers, DuPont's Kevlar (on sale in the early 1970s), current uses, and her later honors. Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Ten new items. Plus E054-10 resubmitted as revision 2 on banked passage CLD-P-ACT-E-000054 (stem no longer says 'profit'). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A Cloudy Solution
Falling Into Place
passages.text:
[1] In 1984, Alexey Pajitnov was working as a researcher at a computer center of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. [2] In his spare time, he wrote small programs to test what the center's computers could {{1|do, one}} of them became the most famous puzzle game in the world.

[3] The idea came from pentominoes, a puzzle in which players fit together shapes made of five squares. [4] Pajitnov simplified the shapes to four squares each and set them {{2|falling, so that players had to rotate}} them quickly into place. [5] When a horizontal row was completely filled, it vanished, {{3|and so, as a result, the}} pieces above it dropped down. [6] He named the game Tetris, combining "tetra," the Greek prefix for four, with "tennis," his favorite sport.

[7] The computer Pajitnov used could not display graphics, so the first version drew {{4|it's}} pieces with letters and brackets. [8] Even so, colleagues who tried the game {{5|found it difficult to stop playing.}} [9] Copies spread from machine to machine across Moscow{{6| and}} then beyond the Soviet Union. {{7|}}

[10] Because Pajitnov had written the game at a state institution, the rights to it belonged {{8|not to him, but to the government}}. [11] For years, he earned almost nothing from it. [12] {{9|Eventually, though,}} he moved to the United States and, in 1996, co-founded a company that controls the Tetris name.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: Both parts are independent clauses, and a period correctly separates them.

B.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: The comma after "and" wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

hints: Can each part stand alone as a sentence?

strategy.explanation: Test each side of the punctuation.

candidates.remember: A period correctly separates two independent clauses.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The curiosity belongs to Kwolek, so the possessive relative pronoun "whose" is needed.

A.rationale: "Who's" means "who is," which does not make sense before "curiosity."

C.rationale: "Who curiosity" leaves the pronoun without a role in the clause.

D.rationale: "Whom" is an object pronoun and cannot show possession.

strategy.explanation: Expand "who's" to "who is" and test it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.D: strong, stiff, and having little weight

candidates.evidence: the fibers that came out were remarkably
candidates.explanation: "Strong, stiff, and light" is a parallel series of three adjectives describing the fibers.

A.rationale: The added clause "and they weighed little" breaks the series of adjectives describing the fibers.

B.rationale: "Lightly" is an adverb and cannot describe the fibers alongside the adjectives.

D.rationale: "Having little weight" is a phrase, not an adjective, so the series is not parallel.

hints: Are all items in the series the same part of speech?

strategy.explanation: Check that each item fits "the fibers were remarkably ___."

candidates.remember: Items in a series should share the same grammatical form.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Testing them in the laboratory, the fibers proved
choices.C: Tested in the laboratory, it was proved that the fibers were
choices.D: In the laboratory testing, the fibers proved

candidates.evidence: several times stronger than steel of the same weight
candidates.explanation: "Tested in the laboratory" correctly describes the fibers, which come right after the comma.

B.rationale: The fibers did not test themselves, so "Testing them" cannot describe the fibers.

C.rationale: The opening phrase would describe "it," not the fibers.

D.rationale: "In the laboratory testing" is unidiomatic and unclear.

strategy.explanation: Put the thing tested right after the comma.

candidates.remember: An opening modifier describes the noun that follows it.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: it is used in bicycle tires
candidates.explanation: "Today" moves from the 1970s to the present, which fits a sentence about current uses.

A.rationale: Nothing in sentence 9 contrasts with the product's going on sale.

B.rationale: Current uses do not replace the product's sale; they follow from it.

D.rationale: Sentence 9 is not an example of the product going on sale.

candidates.remember: Time transitions can move a narrative to the present.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Steel wire is also used in suspension bridges and in the cables of elevators.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why Kwolek wanted to replace steel in car tires.
choices.B: Yes, because it adds another example of products that use Kevlar.
choices.C: No, because it contradicts the claim that Kevlar is stronger than steel.
choices.D: No, because it shifts the focus from Kevlar's uses to the uses of steel.

candidates.evidence: it is used in bicycle tires, firefighters' gear
candidates.explanation: The paragraph describes Kevlar's uses; a sentence about the uses of steel moves away from that focus.

A.rationale: The sentence lists uses of steel; it does not explain her goal.

B.rationale: Bridges and elevators are given as uses of steel, not of Kevlar.

C.rationale: Listing uses of steel does not contradict a comparison of strength.

strategy.explanation: Compare the sentence with the paragraph's topic.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: simply paid attention to a result that did not fit
candidates.explanation: Both sides are independent clauses, and the semicolon correctly joins them.

A.rationale: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice.

B.rationale: A colon followed by "and" is not standard.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, the two clauses run together.

hints: Is each side a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check what comes before and after the punctuation.

candidates.remember: A semicolon joins two closely related sentences.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame
candidates.explanation: "Including" correctly introduces one of the honors.

C.rationale: "Including of" adds a preposition that does not belong.

D.rationale: "Like for example" is redundant and informal.

hints: Which choice introduces an example most smoothly?

strategy.explanation: Read each choice in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the most precise, idiomatic connector.

candidates.subskill: Concluding sentence (connecting to the essay's theme)
candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively concludes the essay by returning to the idea introduced in sentence 10?

choices.B: It all began with a liquid most chemists would have thrown away.
choices.C: Kevlar is now made in several countries and sold around the world.
choices.D: She retired from DuPont after a long career as a research chemist.

candidates.evidence: simply paid attention to a result that did not fit
candidates.explanation: Sentence 10 says Kwolek paid attention to a result that did not fit; choice B returns to that idea by recalling the cloudy liquid most chemists would have thrown away.

A.rationale: This focuses on the vests, not on the idea of paying attention to an unexpected result.

C.rationale: This adds a fact about production, not the idea in sentence 10.

D.rationale: This adds a biographical detail unrelated to the idea in sentence 10.

candidates.remember: A strong conclusion connects to the essay's central idea.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to show how an unexpected observation led to an important invention. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains in detail how Kevlar fibers are made in factories.
choices.B: No, because Kwolek did not set out to invent Kevlar.
choices.C: Yes, because it shows how Kwolek's attention to a cloudy solution led to Kevlar.
choices.D: No, because it focuses mainly on the uses of steel in car tires.

candidates.evidence: One of the polymer solutions she prepared looked
candidates.explanation: The essay traces how Kwolek noticed an odd-looking solution and pursued it, which led to Kevlar.

A.rationale: The essay does not explain factory production.

B.rationale: Not setting out to invent it is exactly what makes the observation unexpected.

D.rationale: Steel is mentioned only as what Kwolek hoped to replace.

hints: What is the essay mostly about?

strategy.explanation: Compare the essay with the stated purpose.

candidates.remember: Judge the whole essay against the goal.

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how a popular game was created and how its creator eventually gained a stake in it. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains in detail how the game earned money in the Soviet Union.
choices.B: No, because it focuses mainly on the history of the pentomino puzzle.
choices.C: Yes, because it traces the game's creation and Pajitnov's later stake in its name.
choices.D: No, because it says that Pajitnov never earned anything from the game.

candidates.evidence: co-founded a company that controls the Tetris name
candidates.explanation: The essay describes how Pajitnov created the game and how, after years of earning almost nothing, he co-founded a company that controls the name.

A.rationale: The essay says Pajitnov earned almost nothing for years; it does not explain Soviet earnings.

B.rationale: Pentominoes are mentioned only as the game's inspiration.

D.rationale: The essay says he earned almost nothing "for years," then co-founded a company that controls the name.

hints: Does the essay cover both the creation and the profit?

strategy.explanation: Check the essay against both parts of the purpose.

candidates.remember: A purpose with two parts requires both to be met.

revision_history.reason: solver B: stem said "profit", which the passage implies but does not state
revision_history.change: stem now says "gained a stake in it"
